text: Towards practical Li–S batteries through the combination of a nanostructured graphene composite cathode and a novel sparingly solvating electrolyte Adri ́an Robles-Fern ́andez a, Gelines Moreno-Fern ́andez a,**, Asier Soria-Fern ́andez a, Julen Castillo a,b, Alexander Santiago a, Daniel Carriazo a,c,* a Centre for Cooperative Research on Alternative Energies (CIC EnergiGUNE) Basque Research and Technology Alliance (BRTA), 01510, Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain b University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU), Barrio Sarriena, S/n, 48940, Leioa, Spain c Ikerbasque, Basque Foundation for Science, Plaza Euskadi 5, 48009, Bilbao, Spain A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Lithium-sulfur batteries Graphene-based sulfur cathode Sparingly solvating electrolyte Polysulfide shuttle Pouch cell A B S T R A C T Lithium-sulfur batteries (LSBs) have emerged as promising alternatives to replace Li-ion technology in lightweight applications, but they still face some important challenges that hinder their commercialization.
To overcome them, several optimization strategies focusing on each battery component have been investigated.

In this work, we have explored the symbiotic combination of an optimized high-sulfur loading graphene-containing cathode with a novel sparingly solvating electrolyte (SSE) consisting of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) as solvent and 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl-1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (OCTO) as diluent, at an E/S ratio of 7 μL mg−1.

The impact of graphene incorporation into the cathode formulation and the physicochemical compatibility between cathode and electrolyte have been evaluated and compared to those obtained for the benchmarking DME/DOL electrolyte.
Using the DOL/OCTO SSE enhanced wettability over our graphene-containing electrodes and hampered significant polysulfide dissolution.

Most importantly, the electrochemistry of this system showed very promising values at coin cell level, achieving areal discharge capacities of 5.3 mAh cm−2 at C/10, enduring beyond 100 cycles with 65 % capacity retention.

The transferability of the system to prototype cells was successfully demonstrated by assembling a monolayer pouch cell which reached initial capacities of 55 mAh and lasted more than 60 cycles, paving the way for real deployment and commercialization of this energy storage technology. 1.
Introduction The ever-increasing global energy demand requires alternatives to the existing electrochemical energy storage (EES) technologies whilst considering sustainability.

Since their commercialization in the early 1990s, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have constituted the most common system for small portable electronics due to their high energy density and low self-discharge [1].

Nevertheless, their theoretical limit is currently being reached and it is insufficient for their implementation in some demanding areas, such as heavy-duty transportation or stationary grid storage [2,3].

Lithium-sulfur batteries (LSBs) have gained attention as potential alternatives to LIBs in the last decade, due to the outstanding specific capacity of sulfur (1675 mAh g−1) and the theoretical high gravimetric energy density of LSBs (2600 Wh kg−1) [4], which makes them a suitable choice for lightweight applications such as satellites and drones [5,6].

Besides, lithium-sulfur technology is promising in next-generation batteries due to the inherent advantages of using sulfur as an active material, such as low cost, wide availability, and environmental friendliness [7].

Overall S + 2 Li ⇌Li2S The sulfur reduction reaction (SRR) happening in the discharge process is a multi-step process where solid sulfur reacts with lithium ions and is transformed into soluble lithium polysulfides, which subsequently continue reacting with more lithium ions, and finally a liquid-to-solid reaction occurs to form lithium disulfide (Li2S2) and lithium sulfide (Li2S).
Nevertheless, commercialization of LSBs is still hindered due to the intrinsic challenges related to this technology [8–10].

The majority of them arise on the cathode side, such as the insulating nature of sulfur and lithium sulfide, the high-volume expansion undergone by the cathode while discharging [11], and the polysulfide shuttle effect [12, 13].

The latter consists of the diffusion of the soluble intermediate species (lithium polysulfides, LiPS) through the electrolyte towards the lithium metal anode (LMA), causing the loss of active material in the cathode and leading to parasitic reactions with the anode, which could eventually suffer corrosion with subsequent battery failure.

To confront these challenges, academia has commonly focused on exploring novel materials for the positive electrode, often overlooking the rest of the cell components, or selecting non-realistic compositional and operational parameters for the batteries [14,15], thus rendering the efforts hollow in terms of their practical application.

Most of the approaches related to tackling the cathode side challenges comprise the design of a carbonaceous matrix that can host sulfur particles whilst confining the liquid lithium polysulfides within this region [16].

Ideally, an optimum carbonaceous sulfur host must exhibit a high specific surface area, adequate pore size distribution, and tailored surface chemistry to enhance its compatibility with the lithium polysulfides and keep them anchored to its surface [17], besides high electronic conductivity for achieving a good electron pathway to enhance redox kinetics [18].
In practice, a compromise between these properties is set, as some of them cannot be maximized simultaneously.

There is a plethora of strategies used in literature to find a suitable cathode design based on different carbon materials [19], most of them involve the use of different carbon nanostructures [20–22] (hollow or yolk-shell spheres, carbon nanotubes, carbon nanofibers, graphene derivatives, activated carbons) either or both as the carbonaceous host [23] and/or as additives [24] for redox catalysis, as well as the addition or modification of these carbons with electrocatalysts [25–27] (metal oxides, sulfides, and nitrides [28,29], single-atom catalysts [30–32] or heteroatom dopants [33]).

These catalysts decrease the energy potential barriers of the sluggish sulfur evolution and reduction reactions [34], in particular the liquid-to-solid Li2S4 conversion into Li2S2 and Li2S, which is found to be the rate-determining step in the discharge process [35,36], and analogously, the solid-to-liquid conversion of Li2S into soluble polysulfides in the charge process [37], partially mitigating the polysulfide shuttle by accelerating the conversion of these species.
However, though effective, these advances in the positive electrode do not lead to a substantial system improvement due to the limited cyclability exhibited when realistic conditions are applied.
Thus, the development of novel electrolytes that improve cell cyclability due to their compatibility with the rest of the cell components is essential.
In this regard, one of the most recent trends consists of the use of sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSE, also known as localized high-concentration electrolytes) [38].

This family of electrolytes outstands in Li–S technology not only because they exhibit a distinctive solvation structure and notable physicochemical properties that facilitate precise regulation of lithium deposition, but also because they mitigate the LiPS shuttle effect.

SSEs are formulated based on the concept of highly concentrated electrolytes (HCEs), wherein an increased salt concentration reduces the presence of free solvent molecules, significantly enhancing stability against the LMA [39,40].
Nevertheless, the application of HCEs in batteries is impeded by challenges such as high viscosity and poor wettability over the cathode.
Addressing these issues, the incorporation of hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) as diluents proves beneficial.
HFEs are used as diluents due to their miscibility with ether-based solvents and their incapacity of dissolving polysulfides due to their low donor numbers, inhibiting the shuttle effect [41].

Besides, HFEs have an excellent compatibility with the lithium metal anode, creating a stable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) which protects this electrode and increases the cyclability of the system as a consequence [42,43].

The most common HFE used in LSBs is 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE), which has been used as a diluent along with DME, DOL or sulfolane (SL) and which has proven beneficial to mitigate the polysulfide shuttle, SEI formation and fasten conversion reaction [44–48].

Considering these strategies for improving cathode and electrolyte, in our previous research, we studied the combination of our homemade ResFArGO, a 2D graphene-based activated carbon, and a sparinglysolvating electrolyte.
This system led to the development of prototype pouch cells with outstanding cycling performances [49].
Still, avoiding the need for the carbon activation process could reduce the amount of time and materials used, which is critical for scaling up.
In this work, a direct combination of a reduced graphene oxide (rGO) with a commercially available carbon (Ketjenblack, KB) was the chosen approach to avoid activated carbons.

KB is a commercially available carbon black used as sulfur host due to its adequate microstructure and electrochemical performance compared to other carbon materials [50–52], and its modifications have provided impressive results, both via microstructural engineering [53]) or by combining it with other synthetic carbons [24,54] or compounds [55].

In the KB-rGO composites, KB would provide the microporous structure to host large amounts of sulfur particles and rGO sheets would contribute to improving the mechanical properties of the laminates, high conductivity, and particle interconnection to enhance redox kinetics.
Previous results on similar systems validate this hypothesis [56–58], where good electrochemical performances were achieved.
Nevertheless, the non-practical conditions (excessive E/S ratio, low sulfur loadings) undermined the practical applicability of this approach [59,60].
Here, these composites are manufactured with a focus on achieving cathodes with high sulfur loadings that are apt for prototype cell manufacture.

To evaluate the suitability of this approach, the physicochemical compatibility and electrochemical performance of these composite cathodes were tested with both a state-of-the-art (SotA) electrolyte and a novel SSE in LSBs.

The SotA electrolyte comprised the classic ether mixture between 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), using lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) as the main salt and LiNO3 as an additive.
Regarding the SSE, DOL was used as a solvent for the LiTFSI salt and 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl-1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (OCTO) was the selected diluent.
OCTO is an HFE that recently showed good compatibility with LMA in lithium-metal batteries [61], but its potential applicability in LSBs has been barely tested [62].

The aim of this work is therefore to explore the synergistic effect between the improved sulfur activation and mechanical integrity of the KB-rGO cathodes and the weak solubility of LiPS in the novel DOL/OCTO electrolyte.
The combination of both tailored cell components would confine LiPS within the cathode, maximizing sulfur utilization, reducing the loss of active material, and extending cell cyclability.
Finally, to demonstrate the validity of this approach, a prototype 20 cm2 pouch cell is manufactured and successfully tested. 2.
Experimental section 2.1.
KB-rGO composite manufacture KB-rGO composites containing 10, 20, and 30 wt% of rGO (hereinafter denoted KB-0.1rGO, KB-0.2rGO, and KB-0.3rGO, respectively) were synthesized following a facile route.

Different ratios of commercial Ketjenblack® EC-600JD powder (KB, Nouryon), 50 mL of graphene oxide (GO) water dispersion (4 mg mL−1, Graphenea), and 50 mL of distilled water were thoroughly mixed using an IKA overhead stirrer and A.
Robles-Fern ́andez et al.
then sonicated in an ultrasound bath.
After that, samples were immersed in liquid nitrogen and then freeze-dried for 3 days.
The dried mixtures were then thermally treated at 800 ◦C for 3 h in a tubular furnace under a dynamic argon atmosphere, thus obtaining the final KB-rGO composites.
KB ratios were calculated estimating a 50 wt% loss of GO when thermally reduced to rGO. 2.2.

S@KB-rGO positive electrode manufacture For the sulfur-positive electrode manufacture, the water-based slurry composition followed our recent works [24], with 64 wt% sulfur (S8, >99 %, Sigma Aldrich) and 26 wt% of the as-prepared KB-rGO composites.
As binders, 5 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose sodium salt (CMC, Sigma-Aldrich) and 5 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR, Jingrui Electronic Materials) were used.
First, a melt diffusion process between sulfur and KB-rGO was carried out at 155 ◦C for 12 h under an argon atmosphere to infiltrate sulfur particles within the carbon pores (S@KB-rGO).
Regarding the slurry manufacture, CMC was first dissolved in distilled H2O, and then, S@KB-rGO was added to the solution and mixed using an IKA overhead stirrer.
Afterward, SBR was added to the dispersion, and after mixing, the slurry was cast over a carbon-coated aluminum foil via the doctor blade coating technique, drying at 50 ◦C.
Then, 13 mm diameter electrodes were punched for coin cell manufacture and rectangular electrodes of 20.25 cm2 were punched out for pouch cell manufacture.

Positive electrodes with two different sulfur loadings were prepared: medium-loading electrodes (2.5–3.0 mgS cm−2) were used for short galvanostatic charge-discharge tests at high C-rates, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests, and also for the pouch cell tests.
On the other hand, high-loading electrodes (4.0–4.5 mgS cm−2) were prepared for the coin cell long-cycling tests carried out at a fixed C/10 rate. 2.3.
Electrolyte preparation The electrochemical tests were performed using two different types of electrolytes, as explained in the introduction.

As the SotA electrolyte, a 0.5 M LiTFSI (99 %, Thermo Scientific) and 0.5 M LiNO3 (99.99 %, Sigma Aldrich) solution in a 1:1 vol mixture of DME (99+ %, Thermo Scientific) and DOL (99.8 %, Thermo Scientific) was used as the reference electrolyte (subsequently simply referred to as DME/DOL).

The SSE comprised a LiTFSI solution in DOL, and OCTO (>98 %, Apollo Scientific) was added as a diluent (1:1 vol) to obtain the final 1.5 M LiTFSI concentration in the SSE, subsequently referred to as DOL/OCTO. 2.4.

Physicochemical characterization The elemental composition of as-developed carbon composites was determined using elemental analysis (EA) technique in a CHNS/O Flash 2000 analyzer (Thermo Scientific).

The microstructure of the powder and the electrodes was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with a FEI Quanta 200 FEG high-resolution microscope (Thermo Fisher) at 10 kV acceleration voltage and 10 mm working distance.
An Apollo 10 energy-dispersive X-ray spectrophotometer (EDX) was coupled to the SEM for compositional analysis.
Nitrogen adsorption/ desorption isotherms were measured in an ASAP 2460 analyzer (Micrometrics) at −196 ◦C, degassing the carbon powders beforehand at 250 ◦C for 12 h under vacuum.

The specific surface area was calculated by the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method, and the pore size distribution (PSD) was obtained from the desorption branch of the nitrogen isotherms applying the 2D-NLDFT model with the SAEIUS software.
The polysulfide retention of the carbon materials was evaluated by mixing 10 mg of powder with 2 mL of a 5 mM Li2S6 solution in DME.
This solution was prepared by mixing stoichiometric quantities of solid S8 (>99 %, Sigma Aldrich) and Li2S (99.98 %, Sigma Aldrich) in DME and magnetically stirring for 72 h.
A 5 mM Li2S6 solution was prepared analogously using OCTO as a solvent to evaluate its polysulfide dissolution ability.
Both solutions were filtered using a 0.45 μm PTFE filter syringe.

The compatibility between the two electrolytes and the electrodes manufactured with different carbons was evaluated through a wettability test by measuring the contact angle of a 3 μL electrolyte drop over each electrode.
These measurements were carried out at RT with a LSA100 surface analyzer (Lauda Scientific).
The drop deposition was recorded at 90 fps and the images used to measure the contact angle correspond to 0.011 s after deposition. 2.5.

Electrochemical characterization To study the influence of rGO content on the electronic conductivity of the as-developed composites, sulfur-free laminates were also cast following the procedure described above and keeping the carbon-tobinder ratio at 2.6:1 wt.
The electronic conductivity at room temperature of the full carbon KB-rGO laminates was calculated by measuring the composite volume resistivity with a 2460 multipoint probe analyzer (Hioki).

The ionic conductivity of the DME/DOL and DOL/OCTO electrolytes was measured from the internal resistance of a 2-pole platinum conductivity cell (CDC641T, Radiometer Analytical) immersed in each electrolyte at room temperature in the 0.1 Hz to 1 MHz frequency range.
The electrochemical stability of the two electrolytes at low voltages was measured by cyclic voltammetry (CV) using a BioLogic SAS VMP3 multichannel potentiostat.
These tests were carried out in 2032-coin cells using a Li||Cu configuration and Celgard® 2500 separator soaked in 60 μL of electrolyte.
Cells were cycled from OCV (around 2.75 V) to −0.2 V (vs.
Li/Li+) at a 1 mV s−1 scan rate, and then back to OCV.

Lithium-sulfur 2032-coin cells were assembled inside an argon-filled glove box, using a 13 mm diameter S@KB-rGO electrode as the cathode, a 500 μm thickness Li0 disk (China Energy Lithium) as the anode, and a Celgard® 2500 membrane as a separator between them.
The electrolyteto-sulfur ratio (E/S) was kept in all cases at 7 μL mg−1.
EIS tests were carried out over these coin cells at OCV using a BioLogic SAS VMP3 multichannel potentiostat in a frequency range between 100 mHz and 1 MHz with 10 mV voltage amplitude.

C-rate tests were performed using a Maccor battery tester at increasing C-rates, with the first two cycles at C/ 20 as a preconditioning step, then five cycles at C/5, C/2, C, and 2C, afterward returning to C/5.
At high rates, the charge was capped at C/2 to avoid degradation and to assess the maximum power output obtained with the different cathodes.
Long cycling tests were analogously performed at C/10 with five preconditioning cycles at C/20.

The voltage ranges depended on the electrolyte used, cycling between 2.6 and 1.7 V when using DME/DOL and between 3.0 and 1.2 V when using DOL/ OCTO for the initial tests, then at 2.7–1.4 V to enhance cycling stability.

To assess the self-discharge behavior of these systems, 2032 coin cells assembled using the KB-0.3rGO cathode (sulfur loading ~ 2.5 mgS cm−2) and the DME/DOL or DOL/OCTO electrolytes (E/S = 7 μL mg−1) were galvanostatically cycled following this protocol: First, cells were left resting at OCV for 24 h, then two preconditioning discharge cycles were carried out at C/20, leaving the cells completely charged afterward.
Cells were subsequently left resting at OCV for different times (3, 5 and 7 days), and then cycled again at C/20.
Cyclic voltammetry tests were performed using two-electrode Swagelok-type cells.

These were assembled inside an argon-filled glove box with a 13 mm diameter S@KB-rGO positive electrode, a 10 mm diameter Li0 disk punched from a foil as the anode, and a Whatman® glass fiber (GF/A) separator soaked in DME/DOL electrolyte (E/S ratio = 33 μL mg−1).
Tests were carried out at 0.2 and 0.4 mV s−1 and voltage was swept from OCV down to 1.7 V and then up to 2.8 V.
Prototype pouch cells were also manufactured inside an argon-filled glove box.

Medium-loading (around 3 mgS cm−2) and high-surface (20.25 cm2) positive electrodes were used along with a 500 μm thickness Li0 electrode (39 × 55 mm), with a Celgard® 2500 membrane as a separator, keeping the E/S ratio fixed at 7 μL mg−1.
Aluminum and nickel tabs were welded to the positive and negative electrodes, A.

The pouch cells were packed in coffee bags (Südpack) and vacuum-sealed after pouring the electrolyte.
These cells were electrochemically tested by cycling at C/10 with five preconditioning cycles at C/20, testing each electrolyte in the corresponding voltage window. 3.
Results and discussion As highlighted in the introduction, this work focuses on the performance improvement of LSBs through the optimization of both cathode and electrolyte components.

Within this context, the combination of a KB-rGO composite in the sulfur cathode with a novel sparingly solvating electrolyte (DOL/OCTO) is addressed to enhance sulfur activation and extend cycle life in a realistic proof-of-concept pouch cell prototype.

The oxygen content of the samples is responsible for an enhanced composite polarity, which is beneficial in terms of the stability of waterbased slurries and leads to favored electrode processability.
On the other hand, an excessive oxygen content may diminish the electrical conductivity of the carbon composite.
Taking that into account, a balance in the oxygen concentration in the carbon composite is required for optimal performance.

With the aim of characterizing this concentration, a chemical analysis of KB-rGO carbon composites was therefore carried out to elucidate the final oxygen content, which is directly dependent on the synthesis conditions, such as the atmosphere, temperature, and time applied for the pyrolysis process.

The oxygen content on the surface of the materials was determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and in the bulk by elemental analysis, which can lead to slight differences in the measured oxygen content between techniques.

As detailed in Table 1, it increases gradually with rGO content, reaching a maximum for KB-0.3rGO, although the differences among the composites are not that abrupt due to the mild thermal reducing conditions, as proven by both EDX and EA.
These oxygen values agree with the ones expected when compared to the specifications of a commercial rGO powder (Graphenea), which contains between 14 and 19 wt% of oxygen.
Once the chemical composition of the composites has been evaluated, a microstructural analysis was carried out to further analyze the influence of the rGO content in the carbon composites.

As observed in the SEM micrographs included in Fig. 1a, as the nominal content of rGO is increased, the agglomerated sub-micrometric particles characteristic of Ketjenblack® are progressively covered and interconnected by the rGO sheets.
The homogeneous coverage and intertwining of KB particles with rGO is expected to enhance the redox kinetics in the positive electrode by creating a favored electron pathway.
Textural properties of the carbon composites were additionally assessed by nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherms at −196 ◦C.
As seen in Fig. 1b, all the isotherms present a type-IV profile characteristic of mesoporous materials, similar to those already reported for Ketjenblack® [23].
The BET specific surface area decreases as the rGO content increases in the samples, reaching a minimum of 1126 m2 g−1 for KB-0.3rGO, in contrast to the 1383 m2 g−1 calculated for the pure KB.
Despite this moderate decrease in the specific surface area values, they are still high enough for the composites to act as sulfur hosts in a Li–S cathode.
Regarding the pore size distribution (PSD) calculated from the isotherms, no big differences were determined, as shown in Fig.
Minor differences are found between the amount of micropores and small mesopores around 4 nm, which are key for polysulfide trapping [63], with just a slight increase for KB-0.3rGO.
Regarding large mesopores (~ 25 nm), KB-0.3rGO also presents a lower pore volume than the rest of the carbons, which is also beneficial in terms of polysulfide retention [64].
Nevertheless, as shown in Fig.

S2, the polysulfide retention tests do not reveal an especially enhanced affinity of the KB-0.3rGO powder towards lithium polysulfides, as proven by the negligible change in the strong-orange color of the polysulfide solution.

This similar polysulfide retention is probably due to the increase in the LiPS affinity of the composites due to the oxygen functional groups balancing out with the negative effect caused by the decrease in the specific surface area in the rGO composites.
To further determine which the most suitable carbon composite was, electrical resistivity measurements of the full carbon laminates were carried out.
The electronic conductivity of KB-rGO-based sulfur-free laminates was measured using a multipoint probe analyzer, as shown in Fig.

The conductivity at RT increased with the rGO content, reaching a maximum value of 3.2 S cm−1 for the KB-0.3rGO sulfur-free electrodes, thus demonstrating that the rGO sheets enhance the percolation degree and successfully provide a suitable electron pathway along the whole electrode.

The KB-only electrode could not be measured this way due to its poor mechanical integrity, which prevented it from electrical contact with the analyzer, demonstrating the necessity for developing structurally stable electrodes.
Once the carbon composites have been characterized, the microstructure and mechanical properties of the sulfur-based KB-rGO electrodes were analyzed prior to electrochemical characterization.

As perceived in the SEM micrographs of Fig. 2a, there is a clear tendency in the medium-loading electrodes (2.5 mgS cm−2), where the number of cracks decreases drastically when the rGO content is increased, to the point of attaining electrodes with optimum structural integrity for the highest rGO-content composites.

The same trend is observed when the sulfur loading is increased up to 4 mgS cm−2 (Fig. 2b), where only the KB-0.3rGO-based electrodes were mechanically acceptable for electrochemical testing due to the reduced number of cracks and delamination.
Thus, it has been proven that small compositional differences strongly affect the carbon composite microstructure, which impacts the quality of the electrodes processed.

The effect of the rGO sheets is evident, increasing the particle interconnection, and the enhanced polarity due to the oxygen content helps to develop homogeneous aqueous-based slurries and mechanically stable high-sulfur loading electrodes.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy conducted for Li–S coin cells at OCV could offer additional insight into the influence of the composites on the electrical resistance of the cells.
For the sake of comparison, normalized Nyquist plots registered for the graphenecontaining samples and the reference KB one are included in Fig. 3a.
An equivalent circuit analysis is developed for each spectrum, and the results are summarized in Table S1.
A slight trend is observed with the addition of rGO, which lightly reduces the charge-transfer resistance of the electrode.
This effect is not extremely significant due to the limited amount of carbon composite within the cathode composition.

The electrode resistance of graphene-containing electrodes is reduced to around 10 Ω compared to the reference KB cathode, which is in line with the previous electrical resistance measurements, further demonstrating the influence of rGO on increasing the electronic conductivity of the electrodes.
To additionally confirm the positive influence of rGO in the electrochemical behavior of the cells, cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests were performed in Swagelok-type cells.
The conventional curve profile of Li–S cells is observed in Fig. 3b for a 0.2 mV s−1 sweep rate.
Two cathodic peaks appear at negative currents, corresponding to the conversion of molecular sulfur to LiPS intermediates (peak I) and then to solid Li2S/ Li2S2 (peak II).
At positive currents, the lithium polysulfide conversion to S8 (peaks III and IV) appears as two overlapped anodic peaks, as expected [65].

Differences are negligible among all the explored rGO-containing samples, but KB-only cathode exhibited lower specific current in peaks II and III, processes associated with the reduction and Table 1 Elemental composition of the commercial KB and the manufactured KB-rGO composites determined by EDX (Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy) and EA (Elemental Analysis).

These differences are also observed when the sweep rates are increased (0.4 mV s−1, shown in Fig.
S4), and they can be ascribed to an enhanced catalytic behavior of the positive cathodes achieved by the incorporation of rGO within the composite formulation.

As inferred from the electrical resistivity and the EIS results, the catalytic activity of the composites would be higher with the rGO content in the positive electrode.

To assess this, Li–S cells were tested at harsh conditions of high C-rates, where the particle interconnection and the enhanced electronic conductivity are essential for improving redox kinetics and the differences between compositions would be more noticeable.
To electrochemically evaluate the rGO effect, galvanostatic charge-discharge tests were conducted in medium-sulfur loading cells (2.5 mgS cm−2) with a DME/DOL electrolyte.
C-rate tests were performed by cycling at successive rates of C/20, C/5, C/2, 1C, and C/5 again, keeping the fastest charge capped at C/2 to prevent anode instability.
S5, all the graphene-containing compositions outperform the reference KB-only cell at all rates, being less remarkable at 1C.
To better discern the better-performing composition at high C-rates, a long cycling test was carried out at 1C, with preconditioning cycles at C/20 and C/5, keeping C/5 as a charging rate.

As shown in Fig. 4a, KB-0.3rGO-based cells outperform the rest in terms both of discharge capacity and coulombic efficiency, reaching initial values of 912 mAh g−1 at 1C and 99.7 % CE, whereas KB-only cells offer just 687 mAh g−1 and 99.2 % CE.
As shown in the voltage profiles of Fig.
S6, the addition of small quantities of rGO tuned the morphology of the second discharge plateau at 1C.
However, the KB-0.3rGO cell overcame this issue while offering higher discharge capacities and lower voltage polarization than the KB-based cell.

The initial discharge capacities are higher as the rGO content increases, and this might be explained by the particle interconnection provided by conductive rGO sheets, which enhance redox kinetics and improve the electrochemical cell performance even at high C-rates, with the best performance offered by the composition with the highest rGO content.

Taking into account the improved mechanical integrity and better electrochemical performance of KB-0.3rGO cathodes, long cycling tests at C/10 were conducted on high-sulfur loading cathodes (4.5 mgS cm−2) in DME/DOL with a focus on the possible upscaling of these materials.
As a reference, a much lower loading KB-only cathode (3.1 mgS cm−2) was used, due to the severe cracking and delamination showed with a higher-sulfur loading (Fig. 2b).
As shown in Fig. 4b, outstanding discharge capacity values are obtained for KB-0.3rGO cells, reaching initial values of 1062 mAh g−1 at C/10 (around 4.8 mAh cm−2) with 99.6 % CE.

Despite the huge sulfur loading difference, these values are clearly better than those exhibited by the reference KB cell, thus demonstrating the improved sulfur activation in the rGO-containing cathode.

However, KB-0.3rGO cells showed limited cyclability of around 30 cycles due to the combination of the high sulfur loading with the elevated solubility of lithium polysulfides in the DME/DOL electrolyte.
This degradation phenomenon is well known in Li–S cells with this electrolyte using LiNO3 as an additive [66].
This salt creates a Lix- NOy-rich SEI layer on top of the lithium metal anode, and when LiNO3 is exhausted, the lithium metal surface is exposed and subsequently corroded leading to cell failure.
The larger the sulfur content in the cathode, the more stress the anode suffers and the faster the cell degrades.

Therefore, it is of adamant importance to develop a suitable electrolyte compatible with this KB-rGO electrode and the LMA while inhibiting polysulfide dissolution.

In the novel DOL/OCTO SSE, OCTO was selected as a diluent because of its high fluorination degree and low LiPS dissolution ability [63], due to its weakened solvating power that results in a higher ratio of cation-anion aggregates (AGGs), as proven by Wang et al.
In order to confirm the weakly solvating nature of the novel electrolyte, the polysulfide dissolution ability of DOL/OCTO is addressed and compared to the one of DME/DOL.
The results are shown in Fig. 5a, where the dark-orange coloration found for DME/DOL indicates a strong polysulfide dissolution.

Aliphatic ethers such as DME with high donor numbers increase the LiPS solubility due to their Lewis basicity [40], which makes them not the most suitable candidate to prevent the polysulfide shuttle.
In the case of DOL/OCTO, a yellowish hue is observed in this test, which is indicative of a decreased Li2S6 presence in the electrolyte, quite distant from that of the conventional electrolyte.
This might be due to the fact that DOL partially dissolves lithium polysulfides [67], which could be beneficial to a certain extent for accelerating their conversion reactions.

The absorbance of both solutions was measured after their dilution with DOL (1:50 v.), and the absorbance spectra shown in Fig. 5b exhibit negligible signals in the DOL/OCTO LiPS saturated solution, whereas a strong absorbance band is seen for the DME/DOL saturated solution.

This test also demonstrates that the OCTO co-solvent impedes the polysulfide dissolution, and the combined effect obtained between DOL and OCTO in this SSE is promising in terms of restraining the polysulfide shuttle as well as accelerating the redox kinetics of the system.
To assess the suitability of this novel SSE, its ionic conductivity was first measured (Fig. 5c).
As expected, a higher conductivity of 7.1 mS cm−1 at RT was obtained for the DME/DOL electrolyte compared to 1.4 mS cm−1 for DOL/OCTO.

The reduced ionic conductivity of the latter is intrinsic to the SSE family of compounds, where lithium-ion mobility is restricted, and this is reflected in a lower ionic conductivity of the electrolyte.

The ionic conductivity of polysulfide-saturated electrolytes was also measured, taking into account that the LiPS saturation point of sparingly-solvating electrolytes is much lower that of DME/DOL electrolyte as proven in literature [68].
In our case, it was found out that the DOL/OCTO electrolyte could not dissolve polysulfide quantities higher than 0.5 M Li2S6.
On the other hand, for the DME/DOL composition, the polysulfide saturation limit is higher, and a 6 M Li2S6 dissolution was prepared.
The conductivity of the resulting solutions was calculated from the impedance spectra, and the results are included in Fig. 5c.
It can be observed that the ionic conductivities decrease for the polysulfide saturated solutions.
As expected, this decrease is more pronounced in the case of the DME/DOL solutions.
At the saturation level, all of them show a similar conductivity around 1 mS cm−1.

The larger ability of DME/DOL electrolyte to dissolve lithium polysulfides represents a drawback for the system, whereas the limited polysulfide dissolution in the DOL/OCTO electrolyte is beneficial for cell stability.
This test shows that DOL/OCTO electrolyte could improve the electrochemical performance in lithium sulfur cells compared to the state-of-the-art DME/DOL electrolyte.
The electrochemical stability of both electrolytes at low voltages is studied using cyclic voltammetry (CV) in a Li||Cu configuration, scanning from OCV to −0.2 V.
Voltammograms registered for both electrolytes show a stable profile down to 0.5 V, as shown in Fig. 5d.
This measurement confirms the electrochemical stability of both DOLcontaining electrolytes tested in this work, where the minimum voltage used for galvanostatic cycling is 1.2 V.
Another important aspect, as commented before, is the electrolyte compatibility with the rest of the cell components.
For that purpose, the compatibility of the DOL/OCTO electrolyte with the KB-0.3rGO electrode was evaluated and compared with the reference DME/DOL electrolyte by performing wettability tests.

This decrease is especially noticeable with the SSE, and this improved affinity for the rGO electrode is most probably due to the increased polarity of the carbon composition with the oxygen functional groups present in KB-0.3rGO.

Encouraged by the promising physicochemical properties of the novel DOL/OCTO electrolyte and its compatibility with the KB-0.3rGO electrode, the electrochemical performance of Li–S cells with a highsulfur loading (4.5 mgS cm−2) was addressed via galvanostatic cycling at C/10.
As shown in Fig. 6a, the results obtained with the combination of a KB-0.3rGO cathode and a DOL/OCTO electrolyte were remarkable in terms both of discharge capacity and cycling stability.

Remarkable initial discharge capacity values at C/10 of over 5.3 mAh cm−2 (around 1200 mAh g−1) are obtained with the DOL/OCTO electrolyte, besides a stable cycling performance with a 65 % capacity retention after 100 cycles, averaging 96.3 % CE.

Regarding the previously discussed results achieved with DME/DOL, DOL/OCTO clearly outperforms the overall behavior of the classic ether-electrolyte offering higher discharge capacities and more stable electrochemical performance due to the excellent compatibility with the electrode and the reduced shuttle effect previously demonstrated.

The charge-discharge voltage profiles shown in Fig. 6b and 6c are initially quite similar for both electrolytes, showing the characteristic two-plateau mechanism exhibited by liquid electrolytes in Li–S cells.
DOL/OCTO differs from the expected no-plateau quasi-solid profile manifested by other SSEs, which fully prevent Li2Sn dissolution.

Rather, due to the weakly solvating nature of this electrolyte demonstrated in the polysulfide dissolution tests, the presence of some polysulfide species is evidenced by the potential well occurring between plateaus, whose intensity increases upon cycling.
Hydrofluoroethers such as OCTO have a low donor ability [42,69, 70], which results in a low but non-negligible solubility of polysulfides.

As reported for other SSE, this type of electrolyte promotes the formation of medium or short-chain lithium polysulfides (Li2S4) compared to the long chain polysulfide species such as Li2S8 and Li2S6 favored in the conventional DME/DOL electrolyte, thus tuning the reaction pathway of lithium-sulfur discharge process.
The different voltage profiles for each electrolyte can be tentatively ascribed to this fact, although a deeper analysis is needed to confirm it.

Regarding the overvoltage between charge and discharge plateaus, in the first cycles it is higher in the case of the SSE electrolyte, but after 33 cycles the overvoltage of DME/DOL increases when LiNO3 is exhausted and Li0 unprotected, whereas in DOL/OCTO the overvoltage in the first cycle at C/10 and the 100th cycle is almost the same, demonstrating an effective reduction of the polysulfide shuttle.

To properly assess the cell degradation depending on the electrolyte used, additional medium-sulfur loading cells (2.3 mgS cm−2) were tested at a moderate rate of C/5 for just 20 cycles and a post-cycling analysis of the fully charged cells was carried out (Fig. 7).
The electrochemical behavior of both cells with medium-sulfur loadings for a limited number of cycles is almost similar, as shown in Fig.
Nevertheless, when disassembling the cells, huge differences are acknowledged depending on the electrolyte.
Concerning the DME/DOL cell, besides the lightyellow coloration of the separator due to some polysulfide dissolution, the anode surface is clearly damaged.

In the SEM micrographs, there are no clear evidences of the positive electrode surface degradation, whereas the surface of lithium metal clearly shows mossy structures, pointing out to the uncontrolled and heterogeneous lithium growth during plating, with possible corrosion coming from the polysulfide reactivity with the anode, which could eventually lead to a prompt cell failure.

Opposite to this behavior, lithium deposition using DOL/OCTO electrolyte is smooth and homogeneous across all the Li0 surface, with the KB-0.3rGO cathode showing the same behavior as for the DME/DOL Fig. 6.

The higher salt concentration together with the lower polysulfide solubility and the nature of the diluent in the SSE allow for a homogeneous fluorine-rich SEI layer and a better plating/stripping behavior for the lithium metal anode.
Besides, the off-white color of the separator membrane soaked in DOL/OCTO further demonstrates that the polysulfide shuttle has been clearly reduced in comparison with the DME/DOL-based cells.
As an additional electrochemical characterization of the cells, selfdischarge tests were carried out in order to check the practical applicability of the KB-0.3rGO cells with both electrolytes.
The typical charge-discharge profile of these tests is shown in Fig.
S8, where a resting time is maintained after preconditioning the cells and leaving them completely charged.
The irreversible capacity loss of these systems was calculated according to the resting time and the electrolyte composition.
The capacity loss is calculated as the relative variation of the discharge capacity prior and after the resting time.
As shown in Table S2, the initial discharge capacities of the DOL/ OCTO cells are higher compared to those obtained for the DME/DOL cells.
After the resting period, the drop in the capacity increases with the resting time regardless of the electrolyte, although significant differences are perceived depending on the compositions.
This drop is more pronounced in DOL/OCTO cells, reaching up to an 18 % capacity loss for the 7-days resting time, whereas for DME/DOL the maximum capacity drop is just 5 %.
Nevertheless, this drop is almost completely recovered on the subsequent cycle, and the DOL/OCTO based cells suffer an irreversible capacity loss of approximately 3 % with resting time.
This value is slightly higher than for the DME/DOL based cells, but the difference among systems is not as significant as it might seem based on the first discharge after resting.
Overall, the electrochemical performance of the high-sulfur loading cells makes this KB-0.3rGO and DOL/OCTO combination approach auspicious for prototype pouch cell development.

An additional electrochemical test was carried out narrowing the voltage window to 2.7–1.4 V to find the most favorable working conditions for the system to operate as long as possible while offering adequate discharge capacities when scaled up into a pouch cell.
The cyclability of a cell operating for more than 175 cycles is shown in Fig.
Under these conditions, initial capacity discharge values of 1108 mAh g−1 and 4.1 mAh cm−2 were obtained at C/10, which is still a good electrochemical performance.

In this case, the capacity decay follows the same trend as previous cells cycled in a broader voltage window, but still noticeable areal capacities of 1.7 mAh cm−2 are obtained after 175 cycles, which is very promising from the realistic application perspective.
Prototype monolayer pouch cells were therefore assembled to assess the scalability of this system.
The KB-0.3rGO cathode total surface was increased from 1.33 cm2 to 20.25 cm2, and the same electrolyte-to-sulfur ratios of 7 μL mg−1 were maintained for pouch cell tests.
The electrochemical performance of these cells with DME/DOL and DOL/OCTO electrolytes was evaluated, and the results are shown in Fig. 8.
Pouch cells assembled using the conventional DME/DOL electrolyte showed interesting initial capacities above 65 mAh at C/20 but they failed after 6 cycles.
The post-mortem analysis carried out for this cell is shown in Fig.

S10, and it reveals a heterogeneous lithium deposition for this conventional system, which can be observed both in the optical images and the SEM micrographs, where the presence of mossy lithium is confirmed.

In the case of the DOL/OCTO-based pouch cells, the one cycled in the wider voltage window between 3.0 and 1.2 V shows high initial discharge capacities (59 mAh at C/10), but it is limited to 17 cycles with a progressive capacity loss and an erratic coulombic efficiency.
According to the coin cell analysis which proved that narrowing the voltage window of the cells with the DOL/OCTO electrolyte (Fig.
S9) led to a cycle life extension, a similar approach was followed for the prototype pouch cells.

The initial discharge capacity of the DOL/OCTO pouch cell cycled between 2.7 and 1.4 V was 55 mAh at C/10, just a slight decrease regarding the wider voltage range, and the cycle life was noticeably improved, reaching over 60 cycles.
A smooth capacity loss also occurred for this cell, reaching a 70 % capacity retention at the 38th cycle.
The average coulombic efficiency was significantly improved in this voltage window, but still lower than that shown at coin cell level.

The lithium anode protection using the DOL/OCTO electrolyte is better than with DME/DOL, as evidenced by a longer cycling capability, but the erratic coulombic efficiency indicates the need for creating a better solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) for further lithium protection.

In a deeper analysis, lithium deposition in the form of whiskers is noticed, which further demonstrates the need for lithium anode improvement. 4.

Conclusion In this work, a novel system developed by the combination of a graphene-containing high-sulfur loading cathode (KB-0.3rGO) and a novel sparingly solvating electrolyte (DOL/OCTO) has demonstrated its real potential for lithium-sulfur technology.

It was found that the incorporation of rGO sheets increased the electrical conductivity of the composites, while strongly improving the mechanical properties of the cathodes and providing oxygen functional groups that enhanced electrode wettability.

Besides, using the conventional DME/DOL electrolyte, the success in this approach for improving the positive electrodes has been demonstrated, obtaining for KB-0.3rGO high discharge capacities of 4.8 mAh cm−2 at C/10, as well as good electrochemical performances at high C-rates.
Nevertheless, since the cyclability of these cells was limited, a novel sparingly solvating electrolyte was developed for polysulfide shuttle inhibition and improving cell durability.
When combining these cathodes with the novel DOL/OCTO electrolyte, the cells showed outstanding discharge capacities of 5.3 mAh cm−2 at C/10 and a 65 % capacity retention after 100 cycles.
This improvement is ascribed to the enhanced wettability and the partial prevention of polysulfide dissolution.
The cycle life could even be extended to 175 cycles by voltage narrowing with a slight capacity loss.
To validate these results in more realistic conditions, prototype pouch cells were assembled, achieving a total capacity of 55.2 mAh at C/10 for over 60 cycles.
More studies including these findings and components optimization are underway to overcome the real limitations of this promising energy storage technology.

Additional strategies could be implemented to further improve the performance of this system, such as carbon surface functionalization, incorporation of catalysts for a more effective anchoring and conversion of polysulfides; and also including additive salts to the electrolyte for an enhanced lithium anode protection and cycling performance.
